title: Canada-U.S. Trade Talks Collapse as 50% Tariffs Lock In on $20 Billion in Goods
excerpt: Prime Minister Mark Carney suspends negotiations and vows dollar-for-dollar retaliation after last-minute U.S. demands torpedo a deal both sides said was within reach.
body:
• The U.S. imposed 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion worth of Canadian goods at midnight Saturday after trade talks collapsed Friday night.
  • Canadian PM Mark Carney suspended negotiations, ordered his team back to Ottawa, and pledged to match the tariffs dollar for dollar.
  • President Trump had declared a deal was reached earlier in the week but granted only a three-day pause before the deadline expired.
  • The tariffs, imposed under the rarely used Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act, cover nearly 500 product categories and carry no built-in time limit.

Trade talks between the United States and Canada broke down late Friday night, triggering 50% tariffs on approximately $20 billion worth of Canadian imports and reigniting a North American trade war that had appeared close to resolution just days earlier.

"I have decided to suspend trade negotiations with the U.S. and have directed Canada's negotiators to return to Ottawa," Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement. "Last-minute changes in the U.S. proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal."

Canada vowed to retaliate immediately. "Canada will match those tariffs dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses," Carney added.

A Deal That Fell Apart in Days

The collapse caps a volatile week of brinkmanship between the two countries. On Tuesday, President Donald Trump announced a three-day tariff pause, declaring on Truth Social that the two sides had reached an agreement "subject to the finalization of documents." Carney acknowledged "substantial progress" but said "important work" remained.

Negotiators had been working toward a framework that would have lowered the 25% tariff on Canadian-built cars and trucks to 15%, and halved the 50% duties on Canadian steel and aluminum, according to Reuters. Dairy market access was another sticking point, with Trump emphasizing any deal would be "great for our farmers."

But the agreement unraveled. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on X that "new demands and walk backs of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days," adding that Washington's offer had included "significant tariff reductions" and "a historic economic and national security partnership."

Section 338: A Powerful and Untested Tool

Trump invoked Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to impose the new duties — the first time a president has used the Depression-era provision for this purpose. Unlike other tariff authorities Trump has relied on, Section 338 does not appear to impose a time limit on the duties, meaning they could remain in place indefinitely unless removed by a future president.

The tariffs apply regardless of whether goods qualify for preferential treatment under the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement, which has shielded much of Canadian industry from earlier levies. The targeted products span close to 500 categories, including wine, furniture, dairy products, cement, clothing, and hockey equipment.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For Indian-origin professionals and business owners straddling both economies, the escalation adds a layer of uncertainty. Canada is home to more than 1.8 million people of Indian origin, and the trade corridor between the two countries underpins supply chains in technology, agriculture, and manufacturing. Rising costs on Canadian imports could also push up consumer prices in the United States, where Indian Americans are concentrated in states that rely heavily on cross-border trade.

What's Next

Carney said his government would introduce "additional measures to support Canadian workers and businesses," adding to nearly $25 billion in support provided over the past 18 months. He emphasized that Canada's economic growth is "accelerating" and that Ottawa would "not allow any nation to determine our future."

The tariffs' legal footing remains uncertain. Trump's use of Section 338 is all but certain to face court challenges, as have many of his tariff actions. Energy, critical minerals, and fish — products the U.S. relies on Canada for — were spared in this first round, but that exemption could change.

For now, the two largest trading partners in the Western Hemisphere are locked in a deepening standoff with no clear path back to the table.
